title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 111
paragraphs: And as he said this, the herdsman uncovered the child and showed it to her. When she saw that it was large and of fair form, she wept and clung to her husband's knees, begging him by no means to expose it. But he said he could do nothing else, for watchers sent by Harpagos would come back and forth to see that it was done, and he would perish by a miserable death if he failed. When she could not persuade her husband, the wife next spoke thus: “Since I cannot persuade you not to expose it, do this which I shall tell you, if indeed the child must be seen laid forth. I too have borne a child, but I have borne it dead. Take that one and expose it, and let us rear the daughter of Astyages' grandson as if it were our own. In this way you will not be found doing a wrong to those whom we serve, nor shall we have taken ill counsel for ourselves: for the dead child will receive a royal burial, and the surviving one will not lose his life.”
